chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Long-Term Debt Cycle, Building the Bubble

lessons.title: The Bubble Phase: Rising Asset Prices, Leverage, and the Debt-to-Income Ratio

body.text: Ray Dalio does not identify a bubble by price alone. He uses a checklist of seven conditions, and the more of them are present together, the more confident you can be that you are looking at a genuine bubble rather than a healthy bull market.

children.text: Lesson 1 explained why debt-to-income ratios ratchet higher across successive short-term cycles. This lesson gets specific about what that buildup actually looks like in the market while it is happening, using the seven-indicator checklist Dalio lays out in "Principles for Navigating Big Debt Crises". This checklist applies at any scale, a single stock, a sector, a national real estate market, or an entire economy's long-term debt cycle, which is exactly why it is useful whether you are analysing a fund's individual position or trying to locate an economy within its long-term cycle.

body.caption: The seven conditions Dalio checks for before calling something a bubble
headers: What It Looks Like in Practice

cells: 1. Prices are high relative to traditional measures
P/E ratios, price-to-book, or price-to-income multiples sit well above their own long-term historical range
2. Prices discount further rapid appreciation
Valuations only make sense if the recent pace of gains continues indefinitely, not if growth reverts toward historical norms
3. Broad bullish sentiment
Media coverage turns uniformly optimistic; scepticism is treated as having missed the point rather than as a reasonable view
4. Purchases are financed by high leverage
Buyers are using borrowed money, margin, or credit, not just savings, to acquire the asset
5. Buyers make unusually extended forward purchases
Buyers lock in future purchases or build up inventory specifically to front-run expected further price rises
6. New, inexperienced buyers enter the market
People who were not previously active in this asset class start participating, often drawn by others' visible gains
7. Stimulative policy threatens to inflate it further
Easy monetary policy keeps fuelling the move, and any hint of tightening becomes the market's single biggest risk

body.text: A rising price on its own satisfies none of these seven conditions. Plenty of genuine bull markets are driven by real earnings growth, reasonable valuations, and cautious sentiment, and calling every rally a bubble is just as costly a mistake as missing a real one. Dalio's own approach is to score how many of the seven conditions are present together; a market showing two or three is worth watching, while one showing six or seven is a genuine warning.

children.text: Applying the Checklist: India's 2023-24 Small-Cap and Mid-Cap Episode

In February 2024, SEBI directed AMFI and mutual fund houses to run stress tests on small-cap and mid-cap equity schemes and disclose the results publicly, after a sustained rally driven heavily by retail SIP inflows had pushed valuations across both segments well above their historical norms. This episode is a useful, recent, India-specific example to run through the seven-indicator checklist below, at the market-segment level rather than the whole-economy level this course returns to in Chapters 5 and 6.

body.caption: The 2023-24 small-cap and mid-cap episode against Dalio's checklist

cells: High valuations
Yes
Small-cap and mid-cap index valuations traded at a sustained premium to their own long-term averages and to large-cap indices
Discounting further appreciation
Yes
Many stocks traded on growth assumptions that implied several more years of unusually rapid earnings expansion
Broad bullish sentiment
Yes
Financial media and social media investing communities were heavily focused on small-cap and mid-cap outperformance through 2023
High leverage financing purchases
Partial
Retail F&O turnover and margin funding both grew rapidly over the same period, though most direct small-cap buying itself was via cash and SIPs rather than borrowed money
Extended forward purchases
Partial
Continued heavy SIP commitments into small-cap and mid-cap funds functioned similarly to forward purchases, locking in future buying regardless of near-term valuation
New buyers entering
Yes
A large wave of new demat account holders and first-time mutual fund investors entered small-cap and mid-cap categories specifically
Stimulative policy fuelling it
Partial
Domestic liquidity and steady SIP flows played a bigger role than RBI policy itself, which was in a holding pattern at the time

body.text: This episode showed a clear majority of Dalio's seven indicators, which is exactly why the regulator intervened with a disclosure and stress-testing requirement rather than waiting for the froth to resolve on its own. Note also what this example is not: it is a segment-level bubble inside one part of the Indian equity market, not evidence by itself about where India's broader long-term debt cycle stands. Chapter 5 keeps those two questions separate deliberately.

children.text: Measuring Leverage When You Cannot See Everyone's Balance Sheet

markDefs.definition: The Margin Trading Facility book: the total value of positions Indian brokers are currently funding on margin for their clients, published periodically and tracked as a proxy for retail leverage in the equity market.

children.text: Indicator 4 in Dalio's checklist, high leverage financing purchases, is the hardest to observe directly, since individual borrowers' balance sheets are private. Analysts instead rely on visible proxies: the aggregate

size reported across Indian brokers, growth in NSE and BSE F&O segment turnover relative to cash market turnover, IPO subscription multiples in the retail and high-net-worth categories, and bank or NBFC lending growth specifically against securities as collateral. None of these proxies is perfect on its own, but a sharp, simultaneous rise across several of them is a reasonable stand-in for indicator 4 when direct debt-to-income data for a specific asset class simply does not exist.

body.title: Early-Stage Optimism vs Late-Stage Bubble Warning Signs

columns.label: Early-Stage Optimism (Not Yet a Bubble)
points: Valuations rising but still within, or just above, historical ranges
Gains still broadly tied to visible earnings or income growth
Leverage proxies rising off a low base, not yet at extremes
Scepticism is still a mainstream, respected view

columns.label: Late-Stage Bubble (5 or More of the 7 Indicators)
points: Valuations only justified by assuming the recent pace of gains continues
New, inexperienced participants arriving specifically because of others' recent gains
Leverage proxies at or near historical highs
Scepticism is dismissed rather than debated, and regulators start intervening

body.title: Run the Seven-Indicator Checklist Yourself
steps: Pick a market, a stock, a sector, or an asset class you follow closely, and score it against each of Dalio's seven indicators as present, partial, or absent
For indicator 1, compare its current valuation multiple to its own 10-year average, not just to other assets in the same category
For indicator 4, check the relevant leverage proxy: NSE or BSE F&O turnover growth for equities, MTF book size, or lending-against-securities growth from RBI data
Count how many of the seven indicators score as present. Three or fewer suggests caution is warranted but not yet alarm; five or more suggests a genuine bubble worth actively de-risking around
Revisit your scoring in three months and note which indicators changed first

body.title: Score the Market
body.scenario: A mid-cap sector has rallied 90% over 18 months. Its average P/E is now double its 10-year historical average. Brokerage reports increasingly justify current valuations by projecting the sector's growth rate to stay at its recent elevated pace for at least five more years. Retail trading volumes in this sector's stocks have tripled, driven heavily by investors who opened their first demat account in the last year. Margin funding against this sector's stocks has grown faster than in any other sector over the same period. However, sentiment among long-only institutional fund managers remains mixed, with several publicly flagging valuation concerns.
body.prompt: Score this scenario against Dalio's seven indicators. How many are clearly present, and does the presence of institutional scepticism change your overall read?
body.modelAnswer: At least four to five of the seven indicators are clearly present: high valuations relative to history (indicator 1), prices discounting continued rapid growth (indicator 2), new inexperienced buyers entering (indicator 6), and high leverage financing purchases via margin funding (indicator 4). Broad bullish sentiment (indicator 3) is only partially present, since institutional managers remain split rather than uniformly bullish. That split matters: Dalio's checklist is most alarming when sentiment is uniform and unquestioning, and persistent, vocal scepticism from sophisticated investors is itself a sign the move has not yet reached its most dangerous, consensus-driven stage. The right read here is a market showing a genuine, advanced bubble pattern on most indicators, but not yet at the point where the checklist is fully saturated, since real disagreement still exists among informed participants.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: According to Dalio's framework, which of the following on its own is the weakest evidence that an asset is in a bubble?
options: The asset's price has risen sharply over the past year
New, previously inactive buyers are entering specifically because of recent price gains
Purchases are increasingly financed with borrowed money rather than savings
Valuations only make sense if the recent pace of appreciation continues indefinitely
body.explanation: A sharp price rise by itself satisfies none of Dalio's seven specific conditions and is consistent with a perfectly healthy bull market driven by genuine earnings or income growth. The other three options each map directly onto specific indicators, new buyer entry, high leverage, and unsustainable forward-looking valuations, that carry far more diagnostic weight than price movement alone.

body.text: This lesson presents Ray Dalio's published bubble framework for educational purposes and applies it to the 2023-24 Indian small-cap and mid-cap episode as a case study, based on SEBI's publicly announced February 2024 stress-testing directive. It is not investment advice, a current market call, or a statement about any specific stock or fund. Always verify current valuations, SEBI circulars, and mutual fund disclosures directly from SEBI, AMFI, and NSE or BSE sources before acting on them.

points: Dalio identifies a bubble using seven conditions together, not price alone: high valuations, prices discounting further appreciation, broad bullish sentiment, high leverage, extended forward purchases, new buyer entry, and stimulative policy fuelling the move
The checklist applies at any scale, a single stock, a sector, or an entire economy's long-term debt cycle
India's 2023-24 small-cap and mid-cap episode, which triggered SEBI's stress-testing directive, showed a clear majority of these seven indicators at the market-segment level
Leverage is the hardest indicator to observe directly and is usually tracked through proxies: MTF book size, F&O turnover growth, and lending-against-securities data
Persistent, credible scepticism among sophisticated participants is itself informative; the most dangerous bubbles are the ones where doubt has effectively disappeared
